article.plain_text:
In November 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT to the public. Within five days, it had one million users. Within two months, one hundred million. No technology in history had ever reached that scale that fast.
Not the internet. Not the smartphone. Not television.
Most people who used it had no idea what was happening inside it. They typed words. Words came back. It felt like thinking. It felt, to many people, genuinely alive.
It was not alive. It was a very specific kind of mathematics, running at enormous scale, doing something that looked nothing like human thought but produced results that were often indistinguishable from it.
The gap between how it felt and what it actually was - that gap is where most of the misunderstanding about AI lives today.
The thing nobody shows you
 
GPT stands for Generative Pretrained Transformer. The first word is obvious enough. The last word is the one that matters.
A transformer is a specific architecture of neural network invented by a team at Google in 2017. The paper was called Attention Is All You Need. Eight researchers. A conference submission. Something that would quietly become the foundation of the largest technological shift of the 21st century.
Before transformers, language models existed but they were deeply limited. They processed text sequentially, one word at a time, like reading a sentence left to right and forgetting the beginning by the time you reached the end.
The transformer changed this entirely. It allowed every word to look at every other word simultaneously and decide which ones mattered most for understanding meaning. This mechanism is called attention. And visualizing it is where things start getting genuinely interesting.
175 billion knobs
GPT-3, released by OpenAI in 2020, has 175 billion parameters. These are numbers - just numbers, floating point values organized into matrices - that determine how the model behaves.
They are learned during training. They are the brains of the system. Everything the model knows, everything it can do, everything it generates is a direct consequence of what those 175 billion numbers happen to be.
To put this in perspective: a human brain has roughly 86 billion neurons. GPT-3 has 175 billion parameters organized into just under 28,000 distinct matrices. Those matrices fall into eight categories.
Almost all of the actual computation that happens inside the model looks like one thing: matrix multiplication. Numbers multiplied by numbers, added together, passed through a function, then multiplied again. Over and over, through 96 layers, until the system produces a probability distribution over every possible next word.
That sampling is where the text comes from. Not creativity. Not understanding. A probability distribution shaped by 175 billion learned numbers, sampled once per word, repeated until the response is complete.
What a word looks like to a machine
Before any computation begins, the input text has to be converted into numbers. This happens through a process called embedding.
The model has a predefined vocabulary of roughly 50,000 tokens - not quite words, but close enough. Each token is mapped to a vector: a list of numbers. In GPT-3, each of these vectors has 12,288 dimensions. That is a point in a 12,288-dimensional space.
This sounds completely abstract until you see what these spaces actually encode.
When researchers trained early word embedding models, something unexpected emerged. The direction from the vector for "man" to the vector for "woman" was nearly identical to the direction from "king" to "queen." The model had never been told anything about gender. It learned, from patterns in text alone, that there was a meaningful relationship worth encoding as a consistent direction in space.
Take the vector for "Germany," subtract "Japan," add "sushi," and you land very close to "bratwurst." Take "Italy," subtract "Germany," add "Hitler," and you approach "Mussolini."
The model learned something about national associations, historical context, and cultural mapping - not because anyone programmed it to, but because those patterns existed in the data and the mathematics found them.
This is what visualization documents about LLMs keep returning to. The internal geometry is not random. There is structure in the high-dimensional spaces these models build, and that structure encodes something real about the world.
The attention mechanism
 
The word "bank" means something different in "river bank" and "bank account." Any model that processes language needs to handle this. Before transformers, this was genuinely difficult. The transformer solved it with attention.
Every token in a sequence produces three vectors: a query, a key, and a value. The query from one token is compared against the keys of every other token. The comparison produces a score.
The scores are normalized into weights using a function called softmax. The weighted combination of value vectors produces an updated representation for that token.
What this means in practice: when the model processes the word "bank" in a sentence about rivers, the attention mechanism assigns high weight to nearby words like "river" and "water" and "current." The embedding for "bank" gets updated to reflect that context. When it processes the same word in a sentence about money, the weights shift toward "account" and "deposit" and "interest."
Researchers have tried to visualize what attention actually looks like. In attention heatmaps - grids showing which tokens attend strongly to which other tokens - you can sometimes see the model tracking grammatical structure, resolving pronoun references, following argument threads across long distances in text.
It is not always interpretable. Often it is not. But the structure is there, and the structure is consistent.
What softmax actually does
Every time an LLM generates a word, it runs a function called softmax. Most people who use these tools have never heard of it. It is one of the most important operations in the entire system.
The model, after all its matrix multiplications, produces a list of raw numbers - one for each of the 50,000 tokens in its vocabulary. These numbers are often negative. They do not add up to one. They are not probabilities.
Softmax converts them into probabilities. It raises the mathematical constant e to the power of each number, which makes everything positive. Then it divides each result by the sum of all of them, which forces everything to add up to one.
The result: a proper probability distribution over every possible next word, where the model's most confident predictions sit close to one and everything else falls close to zero.
There is one extra variable baked into this function called temperature. When temperature is high, the distribution flattens - less confident words get more weight, and the model produces more surprising, varied text. When temperature is low, the most probable words dominate, and the output becomes more predictable and repetitive.
Temperature zero means the model always picks the single most probable word. The result is grammatically perfect and completely boring - the same derivative story every time, the same obvious sentence completions, the same safe answers.
This is the engineering behind why ChatGPT sometimes feels creative and sometimes feels mechanical. It is not the model changing. It is a single number in an exponent.
The loss landscape
Training a model like GPT-3 means adjusting 175 billion numbers until they produce useful outputs. This is an optimization problem. And like all optimization problems, it can be understood geometrically.
Imagine a surface. Every possible combination of parameter values corresponds to a point on this surface. The height at any point corresponds to the model's error - how wrong it is about what comes next in the training data.
Training means navigating this surface downhill.
The mathematics of this navigation is called gradient descent. You calculate the gradient of the error with respect to every parameter - for each of the 175 billion numbers, you find which direction would make the error smaller - and you move in that direction by a small amount. Then you do it again. Billions of times.
The surface you are navigating has billions of dimensions. Visualization documents project it down to two or three to make it interpretable. What these projections reveal is not a simple bowl sloping toward a single minimum.
It is a landscape of mountains and valleys, ridges and flat plains, narrow ravines and broad basins, saddle points where the surface slopes downward in some directions and upward in others.
Where training ends up matters enormously. A sharp minimum - a narrow valley - is mathematically equivalent to a broad basin in terms of training error, but the two behave very differently when the model encounters inputs it has never seen before.
Sharp minima tend to generalize poorly. Broad, flat regions tend to generalize better. The geometry of where you land in this space shapes how the model performs in the real world.
The entire field of research into training dynamics - learning rate schedules, optimizer choices, batch size, weight decay - can be understood as attempts to navigate toward flatter, broader minima. The visualization is the intuition behind the engineering.
The physics that nobody told you about
 
Researchers working on LLM theory kept noticing something. The mathematics of optimization looked familiar.
The equation describing how parameters update under gradient descent had the same structure as equations describing how particles move under force fields in classical mechanics. The loss landscape had the same mathematical properties as a potential energy surface. The stochastic noise introduced by training on random batches had the same character as thermal fluctuations in statistical mechanics.
This is not a coincidence and it is not merely a metaphor. These systems share underlying mathematical structure because both are high-dimensional systems navigating some kind of landscape under the influence of gradients and noise.
The tools physicists developed over a century for studying energy landscapes, phase transitions, and dynamical systems turn out to be directly applicable to understanding how neural networks train and generalize. The math transfers completely.
Phase transitions in particular have attracted serious attention. In physics, a phase transition is a qualitative change in a system's behavior - water turning to ice, magnetism switching on in a cooling material.
In LLMs, researchers have observed what look like similar transitions: capabilities that seem entirely absent at small scale and then appear suddenly as model size crosses a threshold. Chain-of-thought reasoning. Multi-step arithmetic. Certain forms of in-context learning.
The model cannot do it, cannot do it, cannot do it - and then suddenly can, as parameters or training compute crosses some critical value. The field calls these emergent capabilities, and they are one of the most contested and fascinating open questions in the entire area.
What representation spaces actually show
The most striking visualizations in LLM research are the representation space projections. Take the 12,288-dimensional vectors that represent tokens inside the model, reduce them to three dimensions using standard techniques, and plot them. What you get is not noise.
You get clusters. Related concepts near each other. Mathematical reasoning separate from creative writing. Code near formal logic. Language near language.
These clusters are not programmed in. They emerge from training on human-generated text, and they tell you something about what the model has actually learned about the world.
When you trace a single token's representation through 96 transformer layers and watch it evolve, you can see it change. A vector that started as ambiguous becoming something more specific as context accumulates. The word "crane" starting as a generic noun and shifting toward either a construction machine or a bird depending on what surrounds it.
The information is being added in stages. Processed and reprocessed, layer by layer, until by the final layer the representation carries something far richer than its initial embedding.
Early layers tend to focus locally - nearby words, immediate syntactic structure. Later layers reach across longer distances, connecting a pronoun to its antecedent three paragraphs back, tracking the argument structure of an entire document.
None of this tells you what the model is thinking, because the model is not thinking. But it does tell you what the model has learned - which is something different and in some ways more interesting.
The embedding matrix and the unembedding matrix
 
The model begins with an embedding matrix. It is a single table with one column per token in the vocabulary and one row per dimension - 50,257 columns by 12,288 rows in GPT-3. This matrix alone contains roughly 617 million parameters.
Every token starts its journey as a single column pulled from this table. No context. No relationship to anything else. Just a point in a high-dimensional space that the training process decided was a good starting representation for that particular word.
At the other end of the model is the unembedding matrix. Same dimensions, reversed. It takes the final representation vector - now rich with 96 layers of context - and multiplies it back out into a list of 50,000 scores, one per vocabulary token.
Softmax turns those scores into probabilities. The model samples from those probabilities. A word appears.
The gap between those two matrices - the raw embedding at the start and the probability distribution at the end - is where everything interesting happens. Ninety-six attention blocks. Ninety-six feed-forward networks. Hundreds of billions of matrix multiplications. A journey through a geometry that encodes, somewhere inside it, something that resembles knowledge about the world.
The gap that keeps growing
In 1956, the researchers who coined the term artificial intelligence predicted human-level AI within a generation. In 2012, deep learning matched human performance on image recognition for the first time. In 2017, the transformer paper landed. In 2020, GPT-3 showed that scaling worked. In 2022, ChatGPT showed that the world was not ready for what working meant.
The gap between what these systems appear to do and what they actually do is not closing. It is growing. The models are getting better faster than our understanding of them.
The visualization documents - the loss landscape projections, the attention heatmaps, the representation manifolds, the layer-by-layer diagrams - are attempts to close that gap. To build intuition about systems that are too large and too high-dimensional to understand directly.
What they show is not comforting in the way people might hope. The model does not have beliefs. It does not have goals. It does not understand what it is saying in any way that the word "understand" was designed to capture.
What it has is a geometry. A learned structure in a very high-dimensional space that maps inputs to outputs in ways that happen to be extraordinarily useful.
The decisions about how to use these systems, how to trust them, how to build on them and regulate them and integrate them into the world - all of those decisions are being made right now, mostly by people who have never seen an attention heatmap or a loss landscape projection.
The math is not a mystery. It is matrix multiplication, gradient descent, and probability distributions.
The scale is what makes it hard. And scale, as it turns out, is the whole point.

Korea caps coal generation and idles units during fine dust season, while Japan's efficiency rules push older units out. In March both lifted those limits: Korea dropped its 80% cap on coal generation and Japan suspended its efficiency caps for a year. 

Hormuz is a pure gas shock, since no coal passes through it. NEWC was up 23% in March as restrictions were lifted and switchable plants came online but there has been little movement since. Gas has since risen more than 50%, while coal is up only about 6%.

On another note, El Niño is hard to call. A drier India means less hydro and more coal burn, which is bullish. A dry Indonesia means low river levels in Kalimantan, so the barges that carry coal to the ports run light or stop, which is also bullish. China probably goes the other way. El Niño tends to bring a milder winter in the north and more rain in the south, so less heating demand and more hydro, which is bearish. And some of coal's best years came in La Niña, when Australia turned into a swimming pool. La Niña flooded the Hunter and Bowen Basin in 2022, which is part of how Newcastle got to $400. El Niño usually means a dry eastern Australia, so Australian supply should run fine. Two bullish channels and two bearish, among a very, very long list of stuff I haven't considered.  

We're now through shoulder season, so the next few months get interesting. I think coal can still run, but it'll be on India's stockpiles, Chinese domestic supply and Indonesian exports, not gas. Trading Newcastle off JKM doesn't reflect the market right now if you ask me, but happy to be corrected.

Hard to be bearish the equities though. Thungela at a 19% FCF yield and Yancoal at 13% are pricing Newcastle rolling over from here, and I don't see why it should. What I find strange is that the market priced the war shock in March, coal and the stocks both jumped, and the stocks have since given it back. Yancoal is down 27% from March, even though the shock is still running and Newcastle is higher than it was then.
